CHIEF COMPLAINT: RUQ pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient, a 26-year-old male, presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of RUQ pain, which worsened with food. Physical exam demonstrated focal RUQ peritonitis with a positive Murphy’s sign, but no rebound or guarding. Ultrasound revealed a stone in the gallbladder neck and no pericholecystic fluid. Surgery was consulted and the patient was offered outpatient follow-up for biliary colic.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient has a prior history of good health. No past medical conditions or significant illnesses were noted in the chart.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was monitored in the hospital for a brief period and discharged with a plan for outpatient follow-up for biliary colic. The following day, the patient returned to the emergency department with persistent pain and underwent cholecystectomy for cholecystitis.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to take adequate rest and avoid heavy lifting for a few days. The surgical incisions should be kept clean and dry. The patient should follow the medication regimen as prescribed. The patient is instructed to return to the hospital if there are any signs of fever, redness, swelling, or discharge at the surgical site, or if the pain persists.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will have a follow-up appointment with the surgeon in approximately one week to assess postoperative recovery and discuss any further management or treatment options.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with the appropriate medical care and follow-up plan in place.

title: Chest admission
note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient Name: [NAME]
Patient ID: [ID]

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 38-year-old Asian male, was admitted with dyspnea and a productive cough that was diagnosed as pneumonia with subsequent atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobes. Upon transfer to our facility, a CT scan revealed an endobronchial mass obstructing the right bronchus intermedius. After initial treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, a rigid bronchoscopy procedure was performed to remove the endobronchial tumor and prevent recurrence through ablation with a diode laser. Pathologically, the removed tumor was identified as bronchial myelolipoma with no evidence of hematologic disorder or endocrine abnormalities. Follow-up bronchoscopies after 3 and 12 months showed no recurrence of the tumor, and the patient's accompanying symptoms such as cough, sputum, and dyspnea improved immediately following the procedure.
Final Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:

1. Broad-spectrum antibiotics for obstructive pneumonia.
2. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia to remove the endobronchial tumor.
3. Ablation with a diode laser to prevent recurrence.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient has shown a significant improvement in his condition since the bronchoscopy procedure and has no active symptoms related to the previously diagnosed conditions. No further treatment is required, and the patient can be discharged at this time.

Discharge Medications:

No medications are required at the time of discharge.

Follow-up Plan:

Follow-up appointments with a primary care physician are recommended to ensure adequate follow-up of the patient's condition and to monitor for any potential recurrence of bronchial myelolipoma in the future.

note:

Age: 84 years old
Gender: Female
Admission Date: (date of admission)
Discharge Date: (date of discharge)
Length of Stay: (number of days of hospital stay)
Clinical Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted due to her underlying medical conditions including type 2 diabetes and hypertension. She also had a history of amblyopia OD and a resolved branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) in the left eye. During her hospital stay, she was treated with Eyefolate™ capsules and no further complications were reported during the course of treatment.

Clinical Progress:
In October 2013, the patient's best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/150 OD and 20/25 OS. The OS fundus photo showed a large macular aneurysm (MA) in the superior temporal region with exudates. After being prescribed the Eyefolate™ capsules, the BCVA of the left eye improved to 20/20 in August 2014. Further improvement was seen in December 2014 when the large exudates almost completely resolved in OS (Fig. b). In January 2016, the BCVA was 20/400 OD and 20/25 OS, and the MA was resolved as shown in the OS fundus photo (Fig. c) during 2016.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition with instructions to continue taking prescribed medications and regular follow-up appointments with her primary care physician to monitor her diabetes and hypertension. A referral to an ophthalmologist was also recommended to monitor her vision and perpetuate the effectiveness of the treatment.
